title: A Defect Is Not Yet a Scrap Decision
gist: Moh Kolb argues that in advanced packaging (chiplets, HBM stacks, interposers, substrates) a detected defect is only an observation, and the scrap/repair/tolerate/prevent disposition must be an evidence-based engineering decision tied to location, mechanism, accessibility at that build stage, post-repair reliability and economics. The core claim is that yield gains come from linking inspection, process control, repair and product acceptance records, not from higher detection sensitivity alone.

insights.claim: In advanced packaging that combines high-value chiplets, HBM stacks, interposers, substrates and optical interfaces, material and assembly value accumulates as the build proceeds, so the cost of a defect disposition rises at each step.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Raises the economic value of in-line inspection, repair and disposition tooling as package content (HBM, chiplets) gets more expensive.
insights.quote: Material and assembly value accumulate as the build proceeds.
insights.locator: This distinction matters as high-value chiplets

insights.claim: An intervention on a package defect that is inexpensive before die attach can become impractical after underfill or encapsulation, while a defect that looks minor early can become a reliability risk after thermal cycling or operating stress.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Favors inspection and repair capacity placed early in the 2.5D/3D assembly flow, before the package becomes irreversible.
insights.locator: This distinction matters as high-value chiplets

insights.claim: Design-for-inspection and design-for-repair determine where inspection stations are placed and when an advanced package becomes economically irreversible, because repairability is partly set by manufacturing sequence.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Packaging design rules and inspection-station placement become yield levers, not just test afterthoughts.

insights.claim: The semiconductor packaging industry is investing in more capable inspection and metrology that see defects earlier and at finer dimensions, but higher detection sensitivity alone does not establish which observations matter for yield or reliability.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Inspection/metrology tool demand is rising, but the differentiated value may shift to software that links defects to design intent and disposition.
insights.quote: But higher detection sensitivity alone does not establish which observations matter.
insights.locator: The industry is investing in more capable inspection

insights.claim: An optical inspection image can suggest a package failure mode but may not establish its electrical or mechanical significance, so targeted metrology, continuity tests, cross-sectioning or physics-based analysis may be needed to classify a defect.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Supports demand for complementary electrical test and analytical metrology beyond optical inspection in packaging lines.
insights.locator: What kind of defect is it?

insights.claim: Recurring packaging defects near the same feature across neighboring panels can indicate a drifting lithography or plating process, in which case prevention and lot containment matter more than salvaging any single unit.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Defect-pattern analytics feeding process control is where packaging yield is recovered at scale.
insights.quote: At this point, prevention and lot containment can be more important than deciding whether one unit can be salvaged.

insights.claim: Advanced-packaging defect disposition can be framed as five questions: where the defect is (layer, net, operation, criticality), what kind it is (physical mechanism), whether intervention is accessible at that build stage, whether the repaired outcome remains reliable, and whether the action makes economic sense.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: A reusable checklist to evaluate packaging yield-management vendors and fab/OSAT process maturity.
insights.locator: Five questions that turn an observation into a decision

insights.claim: A repaired package route can pass continuity yet introduce different resistance, current density, dielectric spacing, local stress or thermal behavior, so a single room-temperature pass is not a valid reliability qualification for a repair.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Repair-based yield recovery carries hidden reliability cost; watch for qualification overhead that erodes claimed yield gains.
insights.quote: a single room-temperature pass is not an all-purpose reliability qualification.

insights.claim: Package defect economics must weigh inspection false positives and escapes, repair success rate, cycle time, added metrology and retest, embedded material value, downstream yield and field exposure: a poorly repeatable repair can have negative value, while auto-rejecting a recoverable defect wastes package value.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Neither blanket scrap nor blanket repair is optimal; the value is in disposition decision quality on expensive HBM/chiplet packages.
insights.quote: A technically possible correction may have negative value when its repeatability is poor.
insights.locator: Does the action make economic sense?

themes.theme: RDL discontinuity case: state changes the answer

insights.claim: In a 2.5D package, an exposed redistribution-layer (RDL) discontinuity found before chiplet attach may be eligible for a qualified local repair, but the identical defect found after die attach and underfill may require rejection, because a repair qualified for exposed RDL cannot be transferred to an encapsulated package.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Repair process qualifications are build-state-specific; tool capability to add/remove material is not a qualification.
insights.quote: A past repair success is not permission to skip evaluation of a different assembly state.

insights.claim: A package repair cannot be justified solely because a tool is capable of adding or removing material; it must fit design rules and geometry and be followed by geometry, continuity, parasitic/current-handling and reliability checks, with stress testing or qualification-by-similarity where needed.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Repair-tool vendors' value depends on qualified, repeatable processes rather than raw capability.
insights.quote: it cannot be justified solely because a tool is capable of adding or removing material.
insights.locator: If the defect is confirmed and remains exposed

insights.claim: The four defensible manufacturing actions for a package defect are prevent (fix the process for repeating mechanisms, validated on subsequent lots), tolerate (accept within a documented, verified engineering envelope such as exercised redundancy), repair (accessible, repeatable, approved for the defect class and stage) and reject (when inaccessible, unbounded risk, inadequate verification or poor economics).
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Use as a lens on packaging yield strategies; prevention is the highest-leverage action when defects repeat.

insights.claim: An evidence-based rejection of a defective package is not a failure of manufacturing intelligence, because it can avoid compounding cost and quality risk later in assembly and deployment.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Pushback on 'repair everything' yield narratives; scrap can be the value-maximizing choice.
insights.quote: This is not a failure of manufacturing intelligence.
insights.locator: Reject. Reject when the feature is inaccessible

insights.claim: Inspection, process engineering, repair engineering and product engineering are often separate groups with disconnected records, so they can make locally reasonable defect decisions that contradict one another.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Signals an opportunity for manufacturing data platforms that unify defect traceability in advanced packaging.
insights.quote: If those records are disconnected, teams can make locally reasonable decisions that contradict one another.
insights.locator: These actions are often managed by separate groups

insights.claim: Linking one defect identifier to geometry, design feature, lot and equipment history, process revision, intervention record, before/after measurements and disposition lets defect patterns trigger process-control action even when units were repaired, and exposes hidden histories of apparently identical packages.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Traceability across the package build is becoming a requirement for scaling HBM/chiplet assembly.
insights.locator: A more useful operating model links the same defect identifier

insights.claim: Prior acceptance or repair evidence must be re-checked when a package configuration changes, such as a revised substrate with different materials, interconnect dimensions or thermal envelope, because an unchanged inspection image does not imply unchanged reliability risk.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Each substrate/package revision adds requalification burden to repair and tolerance strategies.
insights.quote: An unchanged inspection image does not imply unchanged reliability risk.
insights.locator: The engineering decision should remain configuration-specific.

insights.claim: The right metric for an advanced-packaging defect strategy is qualified product value recovered or preserved without hiding downstream risk, not the number of anomalies found or repairs attempted.
insights.speaker: Moh Kolb
insights.so_what: Judge packaging yield programs by qualified value recovered, not defect counts or repair volumes.
insights.quote: It is the amount of qualified product value recovered or preserved without hiding downstream risk.
insights.locator: The measure of a successful defect strategy
